chapter.name: A Journey Through Indian Architecture
chapter.blurb: Under Theme C, Our Cultural Heritage and Knowledge Traditions. Architecture -- the art and techniques of design and construction, combining functional and aesthetic aspects -- is presented as a journey to a few representative structures, guided by a timeline running from Dholavira at 2600 BCE to the 20th-century Mysuru Palace and by a map of their locations. The journey begins with Harappan urban planning at Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira, moves to the structural stupas of Sanchi and Bharhut and the rock-cut caves of Udayagiri-Khandagiri and Ellora, and then to water structures -- the Harappan trapezoid-brick well, the interconnected reservoirs of Shringaverpur, the stepwells of Gujarat and Rajasthan and the temple pushkarini. Classical temple architecture is set out through its plan (gopuram or torana, mandapa, garbhagriha and murti, shikhara or vimana, prakara and pradakshina corridor), the treatises of shilpashastra, and the idea of the temple as the body of Purusha, before the great temples at Thanjavur, Bhubaneswar, Mount Abu and Bishnupur show what distinct regional styles mean. The chapter then visits mosques and the Indo-Islamic blend at Ahmedabad and Delhi, forts and palaces at Jodhpur, Agra, Orchha and Mysuru, the mausoleums of Humayun and Mumtaz Mahal, and finally traditional courtyard houses, churches in India, the colonial Indo-Saracenic style, and the challenge of conserving a heritage the Constitution makes it a Fundamental Duty to value and preserve.

concepts.name: Indian architecture and its Harappan beginnings
concepts.description: What the chapter means by architecture, why it is presented as a journey guided by a timeline and a map, and the first stop on that journey -- Harappan urban planning at Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira.
concepts.idea: Architecture in India is both an art and a technical field, and the oldest known Indian tradition of it is a city plan, not a monument.
concepts.rule: Architecture is the art and techniques of design and construction, which combine functional and aesthetic aspects. It is not only an art but also a highly technical field, in which India has excelled for several millennia; these accomplishments have evolved in time and developed great geographical diversity. Because the evolution of forms, their endless diversity and their technicalities cannot all be covered in a brief chapter, the chapter takes the form of a journey to a few representative structures grouped in a few categories, guided by a map of their locations (Fig. 3.3) and a timeline that places them in the river of time (Fig. 3.2). The timeline runs from Dholavira at 2600 BCE to the Mysuru Palace in the 20th century. Harappan architecture is the earliest known tradition of urban planning and construction in the Indian subcontinent, characterised by carefully laid-out cities, standardised urban concepts, and an emphasis on drainage, water management and civic organisation. Most Harappan cities were built with bricks because they stood on alluvial plains where clay is abundant. At Mohenjo-daro, in present-day Sindh in Pakistan, wide streets and narrow lanes were roughly oriented to the cardinal directions, almost every home had a bathing area, and used water was taken out of the city through an efficient network of drains; in a large house the servants lived downstairs while the owners probably lived upstairs, where they were less exposed to the dust and noise of the streets. Dholavira, in the Rann of Kachchh, is noted for its precise urban planning and, unlike most other Harappan cities, made extensive use of stone because stone was locally available there.

questions.q: The chapter's timeline (Fig. 3.2) runs from 2600 BCE to the 20th century, and the map (Fig. 3.3) spreads its monuments from Kashmir to Kerala. What do the two illustrations together tell you about Indian architecture, and why does the chapter put them at the very start?
questions.a: Sample: The timeline shows that building in India has been continuous for well over four thousand years, from Dholavira at 2600 BCE through the stupas, caves, temples, mosques, forts and tombs down to the Mysuru Palace in the 20th century, so no single period owns this tradition. The map shows that it is spread over the whole subcontinent and that different regions built differently, which is what the chapter means by great geographical diversity. They come first because the chapter is a journey: the reader needs to know when and where each stop lies before setting out, otherwise the monuments are just a list.
s: The timeline shows a continuous tradition of several millennia, not one golden period
The map shows the spread across the subcontinent and the regional diversity
They are placed first because the chapter is a journey and the reader needs the when and where of each stop

questions.q: The chapter says India's architectural accomplishments 'have evolved in time and developed great geographical diversity'. Using the timeline and the Harappan pages, explain what each half of that sentence means and show that the two are connected.
questions.a: Sample: 'Evolved in time' means the forms changed across the centuries: the timeline starts with a planned city of brick and stone at 2600 BCE, and only much later come stupas, rock-cut caves, classical temples, mosques, forts and palaces, each answering a new need. 'Great geographical diversity' means that at any one moment different regions built differently, and the clearest proof is already in the Harappan period itself -- Mohenjo-daro on the alluvial plain was built of clay brick, while Dholavira in the Rann of Kachchh used stone because stone was what lay to hand. The two halves are connected because the material and climate of a place shape what can be built there, so as the tradition moved through time it also fanned out into regional ways of building.
s: 'Evolved in time': the timeline shows forms changing from a planned Harappan city onward to later categories
'Geographical diversity': regions differ, shown by brick at Mohenjo-daro and stone at Dholavira
Connects the two: locally available material and conditions turn a tradition in time into regional styles

questions.q: The chapter admits that it can only visit a few representative structures and calls the monuments shown in earlier grades 'just teasers'. Judge whether a journey through a handful of examples is a good way to study a tradition this large. Give reasons on both sides.
questions.a: Sample: In its favour, a few examples chosen to represent categories -- stupa, rock-cut cave, water structure, temple, mosque, fort, tomb, house, church -- teach the reader how to recognise a type, which no list of names could do, and the chapter openly invites detours so the reader can go further. Against it, a handful of monuments necessarily leaves out thousands of astonishing structures, as the chapter itself admits at the end, and a reader could mistake the sample for the whole. On balance the method works provided the reader treats each stop as an example of a type rather than as the only example, which is exactly what the chapter asks when it hopes the reader will be tempted to explore more.
s: A point in favour, such as learning to recognise a category rather than memorising names
A point against, such as thousands of monuments being left out and the sample being mistaken for the whole
A reasoned judgement that refers to the chapter's own invitation to explore further

questions.q: Design the two opening illustrations for a chapter on the architecture of your own district, following the pair this chapter uses. Say what each illustration would show, and why a reader needs both.

The second would be a district map with each of those structures pinned at its real location and joined by a line to its picture. A reader needs both because the timeline answers 'when' and the map answers 'where', and a structure only makes sense when you know both: a fort on a hill above a trade route and a stepwell in a dry block are explained by their place, while their form is explained by their period.

concepts.name: Structural stupas and rock-cut architecture
concepts.description: Stupas at Sanchi and Bharhut as the earliest monumental religious stone architecture in India, and the rock-cut caves of Udayagiri-Khandagiri and Ellora, with the custom of circumambulation that runs through both.
concepts.idea: Buddhism gave India two new ways of building -- piling a dome up from the ground, and carving a hall down into a hillside -- and both were designed to be walked around.
concepts.rule: From the 4th or 3rd century BCE onward, with the rise of Buddhism, several new architectural forms emerged in north India and slowly spread to other regions. Thousands of stupas -- dome-shaped structures housing relics of the Buddha or of revered monks -- were built of brick or stone, and the larger ones became complex ritual centres with railings, gateways and elaborate panels narrating episodes in the Buddha's life. At this early stage the Buddha was represented symbolically, through objects such as footprints, the wheel of dharma or the stupa itself, rather than in human form. The main stupa at Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh, originally commissioned or patronised by Ashoka, represents the earliest phase of monumental religious stone architecture in India; a worshipper entered through one of its massive toranas, ornamental gateways depicting scenes of urban as well as village life, and circumambulated the stupa inside the enclosure of railings called the vedika. Bharhut, also in Madhya Pradesh, was similarly enclosed by richly carved stone railings and bore numerous inscriptions recording the names of donors. Stupas are common in Jainism too. Rock-cut architecture developed as an efficient and durable mode of construction for religious communities: by carving directly into the rock, builders created caves for worship, residence or assembly, and these complexes often evolved over centuries, reflecting changing religious needs and patronage. The Udayagiri-Khandagiri complex near Bhubaneswar in Odisha, begun in the 2nd century BCE under royal patronage, is among India's first, and most of its caves served as dwellings for Jain monks.
concepts.example: Many thousands of tonnes of rock were chipped away at Ellora to leave the colossal monolithic Kailasha Temple and the Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves beside it; in cave no. 10 a massive seated Buddha in a teaching pose leans against a stupa, the arched roof imitates timber beams from urban buildings, and monks circumambulated the stupa in the aisle, the corridor outside the row of pillars.

questions.q: Why does the chapter call rock-cut architecture an efficient and durable mode of construction for religious communities?
questions.a: It is efficient because nothing has to be quarried, carried and lifted into place: the builders carve directly into the rock that is already there, and the same work that removes the stone also shapes the hall, the pillars and the sculpture. It is durable because the finished cave is part of the hillside itself, so there are no joints or walls to fall down, which is why complexes like Udayagiri-Khandagiri and Ellora survive and could go on being added to over centuries.
s: Efficient: builders carve directly into existing rock instead of quarrying and transporting material
Durable: the cave is part of the living rock, so it lasts and complexes could evolve over centuries

questions.q: A worshipper at Sanchi passes through a massive carved gateway and then walks around the dome, staying inside a ring of stone railings. What are the gateway and the ring called?
questions.a: A torana is the gateway and the vedika is the enclosure of railings
o: A torana is the gateway and the vedika is the enclosure of railings
A vedika is the gateway and the torana is the enclosure of railings
A gopuram is the gateway and the prakara is the enclosure of railings
A mandapa is the gateway and the garbhagriha is the enclosure of railings

questions.q: The railings at Bharhut carried numerous inscriptions recording the names of donors. What does that tell us about who paid for such a monument?
questions.a: It tells us that a stupa of this kind was not paid for by one ruler alone. Many separate people gave money or stone and had their names cut into the railings they had funded, so the cost was spread across a community of donors. The chapter shows the same stupa being worshipped in its carved panels, so the people who gave were also the people who used it.
s: Many individual donors contributed, not a single patron
Their names were recorded on the parts they gave, showing community funding of a shared monument

questions.q: Imagine you have only hammers and iron chisels and must carve a hall like Ellora's cave no. 10. Using what the chapter says about how these caves were made, describe three difficulties you would face.
questions.a: First, the sheer quantity: many thousands of tonnes of rock had to be chipped away for the caves and the monolithic Kailasha Temple at Ellora, and every tonne had to be broken up by hand and carried out. Second, the ceiling: the arched roof imitating timber beams has to be cut overhead, from below, with the chips falling on the workers, and it has to be finished before the floor level is dropped any further. Third, there is no way to correct a mistake, because a cave is carved out of a single mass of living rock and stone that has been cut away cannot be put back, so the whole plan -- pillars, aisle and stupa -- must be set out before the first blow.
s: The volume of rock: thousands of tonnes to be chipped away and removed by hand
The arched ceiling must be carved overhead and finished before working lower down
Mistakes cannot be undone in a monolithic carving, so the whole plan must be fixed in advance

questions.q: Ellora's complex contains Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves, and the chapter says rock-cut complexes often evolved over centuries, reflecting changing religious needs and patronage. What could a visitor work out about the region's history from that fact alone?
questions.a: Sample: She could work out that the site stayed important for a very long time, because caves of three different traditions do not appear in one generation; the chapter dates Ellora's caves to 600-900 CE. She could work out that the patrons changed, since each group of caves needed rulers or wealthy donors of that faith to pay for it, and the chapter says these complexes reflect changing patronage. And she could work out that the traditions coexisted at the same hillside rather than driving each other out, since the earlier caves were not destroyed when the later ones were cut.
s: The site remained in use over a long period, not a single generation
Patronage changed hands between communities able to fund such work
The traditions coexisted at one site, since earlier caves were left standing

questions.q: Assertion (A): The carved panels of the earliest stupas narrate episodes of the Buddha's life without ever showing the Buddha as a person. Reason (R): At this early stage the Buddha was always shown in fully realistic human form, seated in a teaching pose. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, R is false
o: A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, R is true

questions.q: Compare the making of a structural stupa such as Sanchi with the making of a rock-cut hall such as Ellora's cave no. 10. How is the work opposite in each case, and what do the two nevertheless share?
questions.a: Sample: A structural stupa is built up by addition: brick or stone is quarried, carried to the site and piled into a dome, and the railings and toranas are then set around it, so material is brought to the place. A rock-cut hall is made by subtraction: nothing is brought at all, the builders carve directly into the hillside and the hall appears as thousands of tonnes of rock are taken away, which is why the chapter calls the Kailasha Temple monolithic. What they share is the purpose and the ritual: both house or stand beside a stupa, both are religious architecture, and both are arranged so that a worshipper can walk clockwise around the stupa -- inside the vedika at Sanchi, in the aisle outside the pillars at Ellora.
s: A structural stupa is built by adding material brought to the site
A rock-cut hall is made by removing rock from the living hillside, adding nothing
Both serve the same ritual purpose and allow circumambulation of a stupa

questions.q: The chapter says the custom of pradakshina 'will persist in later classical temples'. Follow that single thread from Sanchi through Ellora into the temple plan, and explain why a custom rather than a style is what survives.
questions.a: Sample: At Sanchi the worshipper walks clockwise around the dome inside the enclosure of railings, so the whole monument is arranged as a path around a centre. At Ellora's cave no. 10 the same walk is made indoors, in the aisle outside the row of pillars, around the stupa at the end of the hall. In the classical temple plan the walk reappears as the pradakshina corridor running around the innermost chamber. The style changes completely -- brick dome, carved cave, built temple -- because material, religion and region change; the custom survives because it belongs to what worshippers do rather than to how masons build, and any plan with a centre and a path around it can carry it.
s: Sanchi: circumambulation of the dome inside the vedika
Ellora cave no. 10: the same walk in the aisle, around an indoor stupa
The classical temple keeps a pradakshina corridor; the custom belongs to worship, so it outlives any one building style

questions.q: The chapter calls rock-cut architecture an 'efficient' mode of construction, yet also says many thousands of tonnes of rock had to be chipped away at Ellora. Is 'efficient' a fair word? Argue both sides and decide.
questions.a: Sample: Against the word: the labour is enormous, since thousands of tonnes of rock had to be broken out by hand with the mind-boggling technologies the chapter mentions, and none of that material becomes part of the building -- it is simply waste. For the word: nothing has to be quarried elsewhere, transported or lifted, no mortar or scaffolding is needed, the structure and its sculpture are produced by the same act of cutting, and the result lasts for two thousand years and can be extended by later generations. Judged over the life of the building rather than over the first year of work, 'efficient' is fair: the cost is paid once, in labour, and never again in repair or rebuilding.
s: The case against: an enormous quantity of rock removed by hand, all of it waste
The case for: no quarrying, transport, mortar or separate sculpture, and great durability
A reasoned decision that weighs one-time labour against long life and low maintenance

questions.q: A museum asks you to fill one display case that will teach a first-time visitor what a stupa is and how it was used. Choose three things to put in the case and write the label for each.
questions.a: Sample: First, a cutaway model of the dome with a small casket at its heart, labelled 'A stupa is a dome-shaped structure that houses relics of the Buddha or of revered monks -- the dome is solid, and what matters is inside it.' Second, a cast of a torana with its crowded carvings, labelled 'The gateway: its panels show scenes of urban and village life, so the visitor walked into the world of the time before reaching the dome.' Third, a floor diagram of the railings with a clockwise arrow, labelled 'The vedika encloses the stupa; the worshipper walks around it in a clockwise direction, a custom called pradakshina that later temples kept.' Together they answer what it holds, how you enter, and what you do there.
s: An object showing the dome and the relics it houses, with a label saying so
An object showing the torana gateway and its narrative carving
An object showing the vedika and clockwise circumambulation, naming pradakshina

concepts.name: Water structures and their conservation
concepts.description: India's tradition of harvesting, storing and distributing water -- Harappan wells and reservoirs, the Shringaverpur tanks, the stepwells of Gujarat and Rajasthan, temple pushkarinis -- and the threats these structures face today.
concepts.idea: A monsoon climate forced India to become inventive about water, and the results are engineering, art and social space in the same structure.
concepts.rule: For several millennia India's monsoon-driven climate has led people to develop a great variety of structures for the harvesting, storage and distribution of water. They range from the simple, such as a humble village pond, to the highly sophisticated, and they are very diverse owing to the different geological, climatic and environmental conditions of the land -- the Himalayan foothills, the Thar Desert, the Gangetic plains, the Western Ghats, the Deccan plateau and the Northeast. The tradition goes back to the Harappan civilisation, with Dholavira's large reservoirs; the Harappans also invented wells that cannot collapse inward under the pressure of underground infiltration, thanks to trapezoid-shaped bricks that lock together. Shringaverpur in Uttar Pradesh, known as Shringaverapura in the Ramayana as the place where Rama, Sita and Lakshmana crossed the Ganga at the start of their exile, has yielded a series of large interconnected reservoirs fed by a channel from the Ganga during the river's seasonal flooding; the first reservoir or two allowed the silt suspended in the water to settle down, a fairly common design, though the precise working of the whole complex remains to be figured out. Wells were built in many sizes and shapes from bricks, stones or terracotta rings, and in classical times a tradition of stepwells, called vavs or baoris, developed in Gujarat and Rajasthan. Temples often had reservoirs or pushkarinis attached to them, used for water harvesting as well as water-based rituals, many of them works of art with numerous stairways built into them. Today many traditional water structures suffer from depleted water sources, maintenance issues, pollution and waste dumping; environmentalists, locals and NGOs sometimes join hands to preserve them, but much remains to be done.
concepts.example: The stepwell at Rani ki Vav has multiple pillared levels and hundreds of magnificent statues; besides harvesting and storing rainwater it offered a social space where people could sit together, enjoy cooler temperatures and exchange all the news.

questions.q: In classical times a tradition of stepwells, called vavs or ____, developed in Gujarat and Rajasthan.
questions.a: baoris

questions.q: A water reservoir attached to a temple, used for water harvesting and for water-based rituals, is called
questions.a: a pushkarini
o: a pushkarini
a vedika
a torana
a prakara

questions.q: Rani ki Vav, with its multiple pillared levels and hundreds of magnificent statues, is an example of
questions.a: a stepwell
o: a stepwell
a stupa
a temple pushkarini
a Harappan well of trapezoid bricks

questions.q: The interconnected reservoirs excavated at Shringaverpur were fed by
questions.a: a channel from the Ganga during the river's seasonal flooding
o: a channel from the Ganga during the river's seasonal flooding
rainwater running off the Aravalli hills
an underground spring in the Rann of Kachchh
a canal drawn from the river Betwa

questions.q: Why did the Harappans shape the bricks of their wells as trapezoids?
questions.a: So that the bricks lock together and the well cannot collapse inward under the pressure of underground infiltration
o: So that the bricks lock together and the well cannot collapse inward under the pressure of underground infiltration
So that the well could be dug to a greater depth in one day
So that the stored water would stay cooler through the summer
So that each brick would need less clay than a rectangular one

questions.q: The chapter lists the troubles facing India's traditional water structures today. Which of these is NOT one of them?
questions.a: Their stone is being carried away to build new houses
o: Their stone is being carried away to build new houses
Depleted water sources
Maintenance issues
Pollution and waste dumping

questions.q: Why does the chapter say India's water structures are so varied?
questions.a: Because the land itself varies. The geological, climatic and environmental conditions are different in the Himalayan foothills, the Thar Desert, the Gangetic plains, the Western Ghats, the Deccan plateau and the Northeast, so what works in one region will not work in another. As a result the structures range from a humble village pond to highly sophisticated works of engineering.
s: Different geological, climatic and environmental conditions across the regions named
So the structures range from very simple to highly sophisticated

questions.q: Consider these statements. (I) The first reservoir or two at Shringaverpur allowed the silt suspended in the water to settle down. (II) The precise working of the entire Shringaverpur complex is now fully understood. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I
o: Only I
Only II
Both I and II
Neither I nor II

questions.q: Apart from harvesting and storing rainwater, what did a stepwell give the people who used it?
questions.a: It gave them a social space. People could sit together on its levels, enjoy the cooler temperatures that the depth and shade provided, and exchange all the news of the village or town. Many stepwells were also spectacular works of art, so the visit was not merely a chore -- Rani ki Vav has multiple pillared levels and hundreds of magnificent statues.
s: A social space where people sat together, enjoyed cooler temperatures and exchanged news
Also a work of art, such as Rani ki Vav's pillared levels and hundreds of statues

questions.q: A village in the Thar Desert and a village in the Western Ghats each build a water structure. Why would the chapter expect the two to be quite different?
questions.a: Because such structures have always been diverse, owing to the different geological, climatic and environmental conditions of the land
o: Because such structures have always been diverse, owing to the different geological, climatic and environmental conditions of the land
Because only desert regions receive rain worth harvesting
Because stepwells were not permitted outside Gujarat and Rajasthan
Because the monsoon does not reach the Western Ghats

questions.q: What connection does the chapter draw between India's monsoon and its water structures?
questions.a: The monsoon delivers most of the year's water in a short season, so it has to be caught and kept if it is to be used for the rest of the year. That is why, for several millennia, India's monsoon-driven climate has led people to develop a great variety of structures for the harvesting, storage and distribution of water, from village ponds to reservoirs, wells and stepwells.
s: The monsoon concentrates the year's water into one season, so it must be harvested and stored
This drove the development of a great variety of structures for harvesting, storage and distribution

questions.q: Why was a settling tank placed at the head of the chain of reservoirs at Shringaverpur?
questions.a: So that the silt carried by the flood water settled there before the water passed on
o: So that the silt carried by the flood water settled there before the water passed on
So that boats from the Ganga could be moored before entering the town
So that the channel from the Ganga could be blocked during summer
So that the water could be measured before it was taxed

questions.q: Give two reasons why an engineer today would still admire the Harappan well described in this section.
questions.a: First, it solves a real structural problem: the ground water pressing in from outside would push an ordinary lining inward, and the Harappans stopped that by shaping the bricks as trapezoids so that they lock together and the ring cannot collapse. Second, the solution is in the shape of the brick itself rather than in mortar or machinery, so it is simple, repeatable and made from the abundant local clay -- and it was worked out some four and a half thousand years ago.
s: It solves the inward collapse caused by underground infiltration by locking trapezoid bricks together
The solution lies in the brick's shape alone, so it is simple, uses local material and is very old

questions.q: A dry town wants to bring an old stepwell back into use. Using this section, name three things the revival would have to deal with.
questions.a: First, the source: the chapter says many such structures suffer from depleted water sources, so the town would have to find whether rain and groundwater still reach the well at all. Second, maintenance: these structures need regular upkeep, and the neglect of years -- silted levels, broken steps and damaged carving -- would have to be repaired. Third, pollution and waste dumping: the well would have to be cleared of rubbish and protected from it in future, which the chapter says takes environmentalists, local people and NGOs working together.
s: The depleted water source must be checked and restored
Years of maintenance neglect -- silt, broken steps, damaged stonework -- must be made good
Pollution and waste dumping must be cleared and prevented, which needs locals, NGOs and environmentalists together

questions.q: Explain how a single stepwell can be an engineering marvel, a work of art and a social space all at once, and why its builders wanted it to be all three.
questions.a: Sample: It is an engineering marvel because it must reach water that lies far below ground and hold its own walls up through a wet season and a dry one, with multiple pillared levels cut down into the earth. It is a work of art because those levels carry hundreds of magnificent statues, as at Rani ki Vav, so every visit is also a visit to sculpture. It is a social space because people sat there together, enjoyed the cooler temperatures deep in the shade and exchanged all the news. The builders wanted all three because in a dry region everyone must come to the water anyway: a structure the whole town visits daily is the natural place to put beauty and to let the community meet.
s: The engineering: reaching and holding deep water through multiple pillared levels
The art: hundreds of statues, as at Rani ki Vav
The social use, and the reason -- everyone has to come for water, so it becomes the town's meeting place

questions.q: Assertion (A): The reservoirs at Shringaverpur were fed by an underground spring that never varied with the seasons. Reason (R): The main stupa at Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh was originally commissioned or patronised by Ashoka. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, R is true
o: A is false, R is true
A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: The chapter's water story runs from Dholavira's reservoirs, through Shringaverpur and the stepwells, to a temple pushkarini at Vijayanagara. What has stayed the same across those thousands of years, and what has changed?
questions.a: Sample: What stays the same is the problem and the answer to it: a monsoon climate delivers water in a short season, so every period builds something to harvest, store and distribute it, and every period builds it from what lies to hand. What changes is the form and the purpose attached to it. Dholavira's are plain reservoirs inside a city; Shringaverpur's are a chain of interconnected tanks engineered to settle silt from a flooding river; the stepwells of Gujarat and Rajasthan add pillared levels, sculpture and a place to sit and talk; the pushkarini is tied to a temple and serves water-based rituals as well as harvesting. So the engineering problem is constant while the social and religious meaning keeps growing around it.
s: Constant: a monsoon climate makes harvesting, storing and distributing water necessary in every period
The forms change -- city reservoirs, a silt-settling chain of tanks, sculpted stepwells, temple tanks
The added meanings change too: social space and ritual use grow around the same engineering

questions.q: Both the Shringaverpur tank and the temple pushkarini at Vijayanagara are ringed with many stairways. Suggest why so many steps were needed, and say what this tells you about how these structures were used.
questions.a: Sample: A tank fed by seasonal flooding or by the monsoon is full at one time of year and low at another, so the water's edge moves; a flight of steps running all the way down means the water can be reached at whatever level it happens to stand, which a single landing could not do. Many separate stairways, rather than one, mean many people can go down at the same time without crowding, and at a temple tank they allow worshippers to come and go on all sides during a ritual. That tells us these were public structures in constant everyday use, not ornamental pools: they were designed around the crowd and around a water level that never stays still.
s: Steps let people reach the water at any level as it rises and falls with the season
Many separate stairways allow many people to use the tank at once, on all sides
Shows these were public, everyday, ritual-use structures designed around crowds and a changing water level

questions.q: 'Environmentalists, locals and NGOs sometimes join hands to preserve them, but much remains to be done.' Now that towns have piped water, is it worth the effort to restore old wells, tanks and stepwells? Argue both sides and give your verdict.
questions.a: Sample: Against: pipes deliver water to the house, a restored stepwell costs money and labour to clear and maintain, and the chapter itself admits that many of these structures no longer have a water source worth reviving. For: they harvest and recharge rain where it falls instead of moving it from far away, they were built for exactly this climate over several millennia of trial, they are works of art and social spaces that a pipe can never be, and letting them fill with waste damages the groundwater everyone's pipes draw on. My verdict is that restoration is worth it where a source still exists, because such a structure does three jobs at once -- water, heritage and a public meeting place -- and only the first of them has a modern substitute.
s: The case against: cost, upkeep, depleted sources and the convenience of piped supply
The case for: local rainwater harvesting and recharge, climate-tested design, art and social space
A clear verdict with a reason, such as restoring where a source survives because the structure does several jobs at once

questions.q: Design a water structure for your school grounds using the principles in this section. Describe three features and justify each from the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: First, a roof-fed tank sized for the local monsoon, because the whole tradition begins from a climate that delivers water in one short season and must be caught then. Second, a small settling chamber that the water enters before the main tank, copying Shringaverpur, where the first reservoir or two let the suspended silt settle so that the stored water stays clean. Third, wide steps down one side with a shaded ledge, following the stepwells, so that the water can be reached at any level as it falls through the year and so that the tank doubles as a place where students sit together -- the chapter's point that such structures were social spaces as well as stores. I would also plan who cleans it, since the chapter blames neglect, waste dumping and poor maintenance for the loss of so many old structures.
s: A harvesting feature sized to the monsoon, justified by the seasonal climate
A settling stage before storage, justified by the Shringaverpur design
Steps and a sitting space, justified by the stepwell tradition and the changing water level

concepts.name: Classical temples: plan, elements and philosophy
concepts.description: What a classical temple is for, the treatises that guided its construction, the named parts of its plan -- gopuram, mandapa, garbhagriha, shikhara or vimana, prakara and pradakshina corridor -- and the idea of the temple as the body of Purusha.
concepts.idea: A temple's plan is an argument: the walk from the gateway to the dark inner chamber is meant to be the worshipper's own journey inward.
concepts.rule: With antecedents in the stupa and rock-cut types of architecture, temples have been central to India's cultural life for many centuries. Whether Buddhist, Jain or Hindu, they were places of worship but also of learning, literature and art -- sculpture, dance, music and painting among others -- and they were centres of social intercourse and economic life; architecturally they evolved into works of art that celebrate life and encourage bhakti as well as quiet contemplation. Classical temples emerged during the Gupta era. Many were built thanks to royal patronage, as evidenced by inscriptions, but also by endowments from various donors. Construction followed principles and techniques spelt out in treatises of shilpashastra, the discipline of arts and crafts largely dedicated to architecture and sculpture. A temple's main elements are a ceremonial entrance -- gopuram in south India, torana in some north Indian temples -- one or several mandapas or pillared halls, and the garbhagriha, the innermost chamber where the image or murti of the deity is kept; above the garbhagriha rises a tower called shikhara in north Indian temples and vimana in south Indian ones. The plan also shows secondary shrines, an enclosure or prakara, and a pradakshina corridor. The main alignment is generally east-west, with the garbhagriha facing east. Temple architecture also rests on philosophical concepts: both horizontally and vertically a temple is planned as a representation of the human body, that of Purusha or the cosmic being, so that the top of the shikhara or vimana corresponds to the head and the platform on which the temple rests corresponds to the feet. The temple thus becomes a symbol of our own being and of the cosmos.
concepts.example: Temple worship can be understood as a journey from the outer world, left behind once one crosses the entrance, to the inner world awaiting the worshipper in the garbhagriha -- mirroring our own spiritual journey.

o: Places of learning, literature and art, and centres of social intercourse and economic life
Places of worship only, with no other function

questions.q: What is a mandapa, and where does it stand in a temple?
questions.a: A mandapa is a pillared hall. It stands between the ceremonial entrance and the garbhagriha, so the worshipper passes through it on the way in, and a temple may have one or several of them. Because it is covered and open, it is the part of the temple where people can gather.

questions.q: Consider these statements. (I) A temple's ceremonial entrance is called a gopuram in south India and a torana in some north Indian temples. (II) The tower above the garbhagriha is called a vimana in north Indian temples and a shikhara in south Indian ones. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I
o: Only I
Only II
Both I and II

questions.q: What does the chapter mean when it says a temple is planned as a representation of Purusha, the cosmic being?
questions.a: It means the temple is laid out as a body, both horizontally and vertically. Vertically, the top of the shikhara or vimana corresponds to the head and the platform on which the temple rests corresponds to the feet, with the parts between standing for the rest of the body. Because Purusha is the cosmic being, the temple becomes a symbol both of our own being and of the cosmos.

Top of the shikhara or vimana is the head and the platform is the feet, making the temple a symbol of our being and of the cosmos

questions.q: A worshipper passes a tall ceremonial gateway, walks through a pillared hall and reaches a small dark chamber holding the image of the deity. Which sequence has she followed?

questions.q: Why does the chapter describe temple worship as a journey?
questions.a: Because the plan makes the worshipper move: the outer world is left behind once she crosses the entrance, she passes through the mandapas, and the inner world awaits her in the garbhagriha at the centre. The chapter says this outward-to-inward movement mirrors our own spiritual journey, so walking the plan is itself part of the worship.

questions.q: You are shown a photograph of a temple in Tamil Nadu with a tall tower rising over the innermost chamber. What should you call the tower, and what stands directly beneath it?
questions.a: A vimana, and beneath it the garbhagriha
o: A vimana, and beneath it the garbhagriha
A shikhara, and beneath it the mandapa

questions.q: A temple wall carries two inscriptions, one recording a gift from a king and one from a group of merchants. How does that fit what the chapter says about how temples were paid for?
questions.a: It fits exactly. The chapter says many classical temples were built thanks to royal patronage, which is known precisely because inscriptions record it, but also thanks to endowments from various donors. So a temple was often funded from two directions at once -- the ruler and a wider body of givers -- and the inscriptions on its walls are the evidence historians use.
s: Royal patronage, known from inscriptions, paid for many temples
Endowments from various other donors also funded them, so both inscriptions are expected

questions.q: Using the temple plan in Fig. 3.18, name three parts a visitor meets as she moves from the outside of the complex towards its centre, and say what each is.
questions.a: First the gopuram, the ceremonial entrance through which she enters the complex. Then, inside the prakara or enclosure, she comes to a mandapa, a pillared hall, and may pass secondary shrines standing around the main one. Finally she reaches the garbhagriha, the innermost chamber holding the murti of the deity, around which the pradakshina corridor runs so that she can walk clockwise about it.

questions.q: The chapter says classical temples had antecedents in the stupa and in rock-cut architecture. Using what those two were like, point out what the temple took from each.

From rock-cut architecture it took the interior -- a carved hall of pillars leading to a focal point at the far end, as in Ellora's cave no. 10 with its aisle outside the row of pillars, which in the temple becomes the mandapa leading to the innermost chamber. From both it took the habit of covering every surface with sculpture that narrates and teaches, the stupa's carved railings and toranas and the caves' carved walls becoming the temple's panels and pillars.

questions.q: A classical temple was at once a place of worship, of learning and literature, of sculpture, dance, music and painting, and a centre of social and economic life. What does that tell you about its place in its town, and about why it was built so large?
questions.a: Sample: It tells us the temple was the town's central institution, not simply its shrine. If schooling, performance, sculpture, trade and public gathering all happened there, then almost everybody had reason to come, and the building had to be big enough to hold all of it -- which is why temples have several mandapas, secondary shrines and an enclosure rather than only a chamber for the deity. It also explains the wealth spent on them: kings gave patronage, as inscriptions record, and various donors gave endowments, because supporting the temple meant supporting the town's learning, art and economy at the same time. A building that does five jobs will attract five kinds of giver, and will keep growing.
s: The temple was the town's central institution, used by nearly everyone

questions.q: Show how the plan of a classical temple and the philosophy behind it fit each other. Use the journey from the outer world to the inner world and the idea of the temple as the body of Purusha.
questions.a: Sample: The plan is a series of thresholds, and each one has a meaning. The gopuram is where the outer world is left behind; the mandapas are the wide, public, well-lit part where people gather; the garbhagriha is small, dark and single, holding only the murti. So the physical walk inward is a narrowing, which is exactly the journey from the outer world to the inner world that the chapter says mirrors our own spiritual journey. The vertical idea carries the same argument: the temple is the body of Purusha from the head at the top of the shikhara or vimana down to the feet at the platform, so the worshipper is not merely visiting a building but standing inside a body and a cosmos. Plan and philosophy fit because the philosophy is not written on the temple -- it is the temple's shape.
s: The plan narrows from gopuram to mandapa to garbhagriha, matching the journey from outer to inner world
The vertical scheme makes the temple the body of Purusha, head to feet, and so a symbol of our being and the cosmos
Concludes that the philosophy is expressed by the shape itself rather than added to it

questions.q: The chapter says temples 'celebrate life and encourage bhakti as well as quiet contemplation'. Are celebration and quiet contemplation in conflict? Judge, using what you know of the temple plan.
questions.a: Sample: They look opposed -- a crowd, music, dance and carvings full of life on one side, silence and stillness on the other. But the plan holds both by separating them in space: the outer enclosure, the gopuram and the pillared mandapas are the public, noisy, festive part where people gather and performances happen, while the garbhagriha at the centre is small, dark and quiet, entered by few at a time. The worshipper passes from one to the other in a single visit, so celebration prepares for contemplation rather than competing with it. My judgement is that the aims are not in conflict, because the temple was designed from the start to give each of them its own place.
s: States the apparent conflict between festive celebration and silent contemplation
Shows the plan separating them: public mandapas and enclosure against the small dark garbhagriha
Reaches a judgement, noting that the sequence lets one lead into the other

questions.q: Write the three panels of a small exhibition that explains a temple plan to a visitor who has never seen one. Give each panel a heading and say what it shows.
questions.a: Sample: Panel one, 'The way in': a drawing of the gopuram with the enclosure wall, captioned to say that this ceremonial entrance is where the outer world is left behind, and that in some north Indian temples the entrance is a torana instead. Panel two, 'The hall and the chamber': the ground plan with the mandapas marked in one colour and the garbhagriha in another, an arrow tracing the walk inward and the pradakshina corridor drawn as a clockwise ring, captioned to explain that the murti stands in the innermost chamber. Panel three, 'A building shaped like a being': the temple in side view with the shikhara or vimana at the top labelled head and the platform labelled feet, captioned with the idea of Purusha, so the visitor leaves knowing that the plan she has just walked is meant to be a body and a cosmos.
s: A panel on the ceremonial entrance and the threshold it marks
A panel on the mandapa, garbhagriha and the inward walk with the pradakshina corridor
A panel on the vertical scheme, head to feet, explaining the temple as Purusha

concepts.name: Great temples, regional styles and other notable shrines
concepts.description: The growth of temple complexes from the 10th century onward -- Brihadishvara, Lingaraja, Dilwara and the Bishnupur terracotta temples -- the skills and mathematics behind them, and four notable shrines at Sharada Peetha, Hidimba Devi, Jageshwar and the Golden Temple.
concepts.idea: The same idea of a temple takes a different body in every region, because the stone, the brick and the craft of each place decide what the idea can be made of.
concepts.rule: Until the 8th or 9th century temples were modest in size; from the 10th century onward, in different parts of India, they grew in scale and began incorporating multiple shrines, amenities and enclosures or prakaras, culminating in vast complexes. The Brihadishvara Temple at Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu was built by Rajaraja Chola I around 1010 and is renowned for its vast mandapas, a huge vimana over 60 metres high, a massive Nandi or sacred bull carved from a single stone sitting in a pavilion facing the main shrine, and intricate granite carvings. The Lingaraja Temple at Bhubaneswar in Odisha, built in the early 11th century, has three large mandapas used for different purposes and is built from locally available sandstone and laterite; both it and the Brihadishvara Temple are dedicated to Shiva, with several secondary shrines dedicated to Parvati and other deities. The Dilwara Temples at Mount Abu in Rajasthan are a group of five exquisitely carved Jain temples built between the 11th and 13th centuries by the Solanki or Chaulukya dynasty, made of white marble procured from the nearby Aravalli hills, with carvings of the Jain tirthankaras, deities, dancers, musicians and ornamental patterns covering every surface. The terracotta temples of Bishnupur in West Bengal, built in the 17th and 18th centuries, are brick structures whose square panels, first carved by hand and then fired in a kiln in a precise manner, depict themes associated with Radha, Krishna or Rama and scenes from everyday life. Besides large manpower and accomplished sculptors, such architecture required highly skilled architects, engineers and craftsmen, and recent studies show that the planning involved a good deal of mathematics, especially advanced geometry -- as is also true of Egypt's pyramids and temples, Athens' Parthenon and medieval Europe's gothic cathedrals.
concepts.example: Four further shrines are singled out: Sharada Peetha in Jammu and Kashmir, a renowned centre of learning and a key site in the development of the Sharada script; the 16th-century Hidimba Devi Temple at Manali; the Jageshwar group of about 124 stone temples in Uttarakhand; and the Harmandir Sahib or Golden Temple in Punjab, the holiest of the Sikh shrines.

questions.q: A craftsman at Bishnupur and a craftsman at Dilwara are each asked to make a decorated panel. Describe how their work would differ, and say what decides the difference.
questions.a: The Dilwara craftsman cuts into white marble brought from the nearby Aravalli hills; his work is subtractive, done once and directly on the finished surface, and the result is delicate carving of tirthankaras, deities, dancers, musicians and ornament covering every surface. The Bishnupur craftsman works in clay: he carves the square panel by hand first and then fires it in a kiln in a precise manner, so the panel is made separately and afterwards set into a brick wall, and his subjects are Radha, Krishna or Rama and scenes of everyday life. What decides the difference is the material each region offers -- marble in the Aravallis, clay in Bengal's delta -- which is what the chapter means by distinct regional styles.
s: Dilwara: carving directly into white marble from the nearby Aravalli hills, covering every surface
Bishnupur: panels of clay carved by hand, then fired in a kiln and set into brick walls
The locally available material, and hence the regional style, decides the difference

questions.q: The chapter notes both that planning a classical temple involved a good deal of mathematics, especially advanced geometry, and that none of the structures discussed so far used any cement mortar. Explain why those two facts belong together.
questions.a: Sample: If there is no mortar, nothing glues the building together; every block has to hold its neighbours by its own weight and by the exactness of its cut. That makes the geometry not an ornament but the structure itself -- angles, proportions and the size of each stone must be worked out before a single block is dressed, because a stone that is wrong cannot be packed out with mortar afterwards. It also explains why such work needed highly skilled architects, engineers and craftsmen as well as large manpower: the calculation and the cutting have to match, and a huge vimana over 60 metres high stands only if they do.
s: Without mortar, stability comes from the weight and exact cut of each block
So the geometry must be settled in advance, since errors cannot be corrected with mortar
This explains the need for skilled architects, engineers and craftsmen alongside large manpower

questions.q: This section visits temples in Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Rajasthan and West Bengal. Using their materials and their carving, explain what the chapter means by 'distinct regional styles'.
questions.a: Sample: In Tamil Nadu the Brihadishvara Temple is granite, with a huge pyramidal vimana over 60 metres high and carving cut into a very hard stone. In Odisha the Lingaraja Temple uses locally available sandstone and laterite, has three large mandapas for different purposes, and is rich in ornate carving on a softer stone. In Rajasthan the Dilwara group is white marble from the nearby Aravalli hills, and the softness and whiteness of marble allow carving so delicate that it covers every surface. In West Bengal, where there is clay rather than good building stone, Bishnupur's temples are of brick and their decoration is terracotta panels carved by hand and fired. So a regional style is what happens when one religious idea meets the material, the climate and the craft of a particular place.
s: Contrasts at least three of the four materials: granite, sandstone and laterite, marble, brick and terracotta
Links each material to the kind of carving or form it allows
Concludes that regional style is the same idea shaped by local material and craft

questions.q: The chapter sets Indian temple building beside Egypt's pyramids and temples, Athens' Parthenon and medieval Europe's gothic cathedrals. What is it arguing by putting them together, and what does the comparison add for a reader?
questions.a: Sample: It is arguing that large sacred building anywhere demands the same things -- a large workforce, accomplished sculptors, highly skilled architects and engineers, elaborate construction techniques, and a good deal of mathematics, especially advanced geometry. By naming three famous non-Indian examples the chapter makes the point that Indian temples are not an exotic special case to be admired for their strangeness, but part of a worldwide class of achievement that can be judged by the same measures. For the reader it does two things: it removes the temptation to think this skill was unique to India, and it removes the opposite temptation to think advanced engineering only ever happened elsewhere. It also lets the reader carry the same questions -- what material, whose labour, what geometry -- to any great building she meets.
s: The shared requirement of manpower, skilled architects and engineers, and advanced geometry
The argument that Indian temples belong to a worldwide class of achievement judged by the same measures
What it adds for the reader: a common set of questions to ask of any great sacred building

questions.q: Sharada Peetha is now in ruins, yet the chapter says it remains an important part of India's archaeological and cultural heritage. Can a ruin still matter as much as a building in use? Argue and decide.
questions.a: Sample: Against: a ruin no longer does the job it was built for -- Sharada Peetha is not now teaching anyone, and a living shrine like the Golden Temple or Jageshwar carries its tradition forward every day. For: the ruin is still evidence, and archaeology reads what is left of the walls and the site in ways no restored building allows; its history is not undone by its collapse, since it was a centre of learning that drew scholars from India and abroad and was key to the development of the Sharada script, and Kashmir's name Sharada Desh still carries that memory. My decision is that a ruin matters differently rather than less: a working shrine keeps a practice alive, while a ruin keeps a record, and a country that wants to understand itself needs both.
s: The case against: a ruin no longer performs its original function
The case for: it survives as archaeological evidence and as a recorded history, including the Sharada script and the name Sharada Desh
A clear decision, distinguishing keeping a practice alive from keeping a record

questions.q: A gallery called 'Temples of India' has room for only four exhibits, one from each of four regions in this section. Choose them and justify each choice.
questions.a: Sample: First, a scale model of the Brihadishvara vimana with a figure beside it for height, for Tamil Nadu, because the leap in scale from the 10th century onward is the single biggest change this section records. Second, a cast of an ornate carving from the Lingaraja Temple with a sample of sandstone and laterite beside it, for Odisha, to show how a softer local stone shapes the carving. Third, a lit marble panel from Dilwara showing tirthankaras, dancers and musicians, for Rajasthan, because it demonstrates what white marble from the Aravallis allows a carver to attempt. Fourth, an unfired clay panel next to a fired terracotta one from Bishnupur, for West Bengal, because the pair shows the one technique in this section where the decoration is made before it is ever put on the building. Together the four say the same thing in four materials: the idea is shared, the substance is local.
s: A southern exhibit showing scale, such as the Brihadishvara vimana

A Bengal exhibit showing the terracotta process, with a justification tying all four to local material

concepts.name: The architecture of mosques and the Indo-Islamic blend
concepts.description: What a mosque is for and how it is arranged -- prayer hall, domes, minarets and mihrab -- the Jama Masjids of Ahmedabad and Delhi, and the features that make up what has been called Indo-Islamic architecture.
concepts.idea: A mosque must point at Mecca and gather a crowd; everything else about it -- the stone, the carving, the balconies -- was supplied by the place it was built in.
concepts.rule: Mosques are places of worship where followers of Islam gather for prayer; they also serve as centres for religious education, community gatherings, and venues for lectures and discussions. A mosque has a prayer hall oriented towards Mecca, the most sacred site in Islam, located in Saudi Arabia, and the niche in the wall that points to that direction is the mihrab. Larger mosques often include one or several domes and minarets -- towers on either side of the domes, from where the muezzin makes his call to prayer. Friday prayers are especially important in Islam, and the large mosques where these are held are often called Jama Masjid: jama means gathering or assembly, masjid means mosque. The Jama Masjid in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, was built by Sultan Ahmed Shah I in the 15th century, of yellow sandstone, and blends Hindu and Islamic architectural elements; its facade shows elegant arches and the bases of two minarets, whose top portions were destroyed in earthquakes and survive only in a sketch made in 1809 by a British army officer. Intricate stone jalis or latticed screens, pillars of the same style as in some temples but without decorations, and detailed carvings have led scholars to suggest that the mosque was built with the help of local Hindu and Jain artisans, masons and stone carvers. This is not uncommon in what has been called Indo-Islamic architecture, which blends Islamic building traditions with Indian craftsmanship; its features include domes, arches both pointed and corbelled, jalis and floral motifs, and in Rajasthan local features such as ornate jharokhas, or overhanging balconies, and chhatris, or pavilion domes, were often integrated. Corbelled construction means stacking blocks as in a staircase pattern.
concepts.example: The Jama Masjid in Delhi, India's largest mosque, was built by Shah Jahan in the mid-17th century after he moved his capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad; about 5,000 workers were pressed into service, it is of red sandstone with white marble decorations, it has three large entrances, two 40-metre tall minarets and three large domes over the prayer hall, its courtyard holds up to 25,000 people, and its walls and arches carry calligraphy of verses from the Quran.

questions.q: In one mosque a visitor notices pointed arches, intricate stone jalis, pillars in a temple style but left plain, and floral motifs. Explain what she is looking at, using the chapter's own term.
questions.a: She is looking at Indo-Islamic architecture, which the chapter describes as a blend of Islamic building traditions with Indian craftsmanship. The pointed arches, the domes and the floral motifs come from the Islamic tradition; the jalis and the temple-style pillars come from Indian craft practice, and the fact that those pillars are left without decoration shows the craftsmen adapting their usual work to a new setting. questions.q: A mosque's prayer hall must face Mecca, while a classical temple is generally aligned east-west with the garbhagriha facing east. Compare what each rule means for the builder choosing how to set the building on its ground.
questions.a: Sample: For the temple the rule is fixed and the same everywhere in India: the main alignment is east-west with the garbhagriha facing east, so a builder in Tamil Nadu and a builder in Odisha turn their plans the same way. For the mosque the rule is fixed in a different sense -- it points at one real place on the earth, Mecca in Saudi Arabia -- so the direction depends on where the mosque itself stands, and the mihrab in the wall marks it for the worshippers inside. The consequence is that a temple's orientation follows the sun while a mosque's follows a point on the map, and the mosque builder must work his direction out for each new site before he can lay out the prayer hall at all.
s: The temple rule: east-west alignment with the garbhagriha facing east, the same everywhere
The mosque rule: the prayer hall faces Mecca, marked inside by the mihrab, so the direction depends on the site
The consequence: one orientation follows the sun, the other must be calculated afresh for each place

questions.q: What exactly does the term 'Indo-Islamic architecture' describe, and what evidence in this section supports using it?
questions.a: Sample: It describes buildings that blend Islamic building traditions with Indian craftsmanship, rather than either tradition on its own. The chapter's list of its features shows the blend: domes, arches both pointed and corbelled, jalis and floral motifs, with regional additions such as Rajasthan's jharokhas and chhatris. The Ahmedabad Jama Masjid is the evidence: it is a mosque in plan and purpose, with a prayer hall, minarets and elegant arches, yet its yellow sandstone is local, its jalis are intricate stone latticework of a kind Indian carvers had long made, and its pillars are of the same style found in some temples though left undecorated. Because those skills belonged to the region and not to the design, scholars suggest local Hindu and Jain artisans, masons and stone carvers built it -- which is precisely what the term is meant to capture.
s: The term means a blend of Islamic building traditions with Indian craftsmanship
Lists the blended features: domes, pointed and corbelled arches, jalis, floral motifs, jharokhas and chhatris
Cites the Ahmedabad evidence -- local sandstone, jalis, temple-style plain pillars -- and the conclusion about local artisans

questions.q: Compare the Jama Masjid of Ahmedabad with the Jama Masjid of Delhi -- patron, period, material and scale -- and say what each building tells us about the power behind it.
questions.a: Sample: Ahmedabad's was built by Sultan Ahmed Shah I in the 15th century, in the yellow sandstone of Gujarat, with elegant arches, stone jalis and two minarets whose tops earthquakes have since taken; its architecture took on a strong regional flavour and blends Hindu and Islamic elements. Delhi's was built by Shah Jahan in the mid-17th century, of red sandstone with white marble decorations, with three large entrances, three domes, two 40-metre minarets and a courtyard for 25,000 people, using about 5,000 workers. The Ahmedabad mosque speaks of a regional sultanate building with its own province's stone and its own province's craftsmen. The Delhi mosque speaks of an empire: a ruler who had just moved his capital, who could command thousands of workers and bring marble to face his sandstone, and who wanted the whole city's Muslims gathered in one courtyard. Scale and material, in other words, are a measure of reach.
s: Ahmedabad: Sultan Ahmed Shah I, 15th century, local yellow sandstone, regional blend of elements
Delhi: Shah Jahan, mid-17th century, red sandstone with marble, 5,000 workers, courtyard for 25,000
Draws the conclusion: a regional sultanate against an empire, with scale and material as the measure of reach

questions.q: The chapter says features of the Ahmedabad mosque 'have led scholars to suggest' that local Hindu and Jain artisans built it. How strong is that evidence? Judge, and say why the chapter uses the word 'suggest'.
questions.a: Sample: The evidence is good but indirect. In its favour, three separate details point the same way -- intricate stone jalis, pillars of a style found in some temples, and detailed carvings -- and craft habits of that kind are hard to fake, since a carver works the way he was trained. Against it, none of this is a signature: no inscription names the masons, and a visiting workshop could in principle have imitated local forms. That is why the chapter writes 'suggest' rather than 'prove'. My judgement is that the inference is a sound one for a textbook to make, because it rests on several independent features rather than one, and because the chapter is careful to present it as what scholars think rather than as a settled fact.
s: The strength: several independent craft details point the same way, and craft habits reflect training
The weakness: no inscription or direct record names the craftsmen
Explains the word 'suggest' and reaches a judgement about how far the inference can be trusted

questions.q: Write a three-stop trail guide for schoolchildren visiting a large mosque. For each stop, say what to look at and what question to ask there.
questions.a: Sample: Stop one, the courtyard: look at its size and its paving, and ask how many people it was meant to hold and for which day, since Friday prayers are especially important and it is the gathering they are built for -- Delhi's courtyard takes 25,000. Stop two, the facade and the minarets: look at the material, the arches and any latticed jali screens, and ask what stone this is and where it came from, because local stone and local carving are the clue to who actually built it. Stop three, inside the prayer hall at the mihrab: look at the niche in the wall and at the calligraphy around it, and ask which direction this wall faces and why -- the answer, Mecca, explains the whole orientation of the building, and the calligraphy of verses from the Quran explains its decoration.
s: A stop at the courtyard, about capacity and congregational gathering
A stop at the facade or minarets, about material, arches, jalis and who built them
A stop at the mihrab, about orientation towards Mecca and calligraphic decoration

concepts.name: Forts and palaces
concepts.description: Why forts were sited where they were and what they contained, and the four examples the chapter visits -- Mehrangarh at Jodhpur, the Red Fort at Agra, the Orchha fort-palace complex and the Mysuru Palace.
concepts.idea: A fort had to defend a kingdom and house a court at the same time, so its plan is a record of both the enemy outside and the household inside.
concepts.rule: Forts protected a kingdom from the onslaught of invaders. They were therefore strategically located near important land or sea routes, and often atop a hill so as to command a view of the plains below. Forts also accommodated the residences of the ruling and military classes, and in some cases even an entire city, depending on their size; because some sheltered a royal palace, forts and palaces are treated together. Construction of the Mehrangarh Fort in Rajasthan began in the mid-15th century and Rajput rulers went on expanding it for the next two centuries or so; overlooking Jodhpur, it is built of massive blocks of locally sourced red sandstone, and the palace within it has several areas for royalty, separate quarters for men and women, living quarters for the staff, and stables and barracks. Many parts of the fort are now a museum. The Red Fort at Agra, not to be confused with Delhi's Red Fort, was originally of brick and had fallen to ruin when Akbar decided to make his capital there and rebuild it, with palaces and gardens, living quarters, and halls for public and private audiences; its name comes from the red sandstone mined at Dholpur in Rajasthan, some 60 km away. Akbar's grandson Shah Jahan was fond of marble and replaced many of the sandstone buildings with marble ones, in particular the palaces, and he was imprisoned until his death in one of them by his son Aurangzeb; many of the fort's buildings were destroyed by British troops of the East India Company in the 19th century.
concepts.example: The Orchha fort-palace complex, built in the mid-16th century by the Bundela Rajput kings on the banks of the Betwa in Madhya Pradesh, holds three main palaces -- Raja Mahal, Jahangir Mahal and Rai Praveen Mahal -- with chhatris on the riverbank, while the Mysuru Palace, also called Amba Vilas Palace, is a 20th-century Indo-Saracenic building of the Wadiyar dynasty, lit by nearly 100,000 lights on Sunday evenings and during festivals.

questions.q: Why does the chapter club forts and palaces together in one category?
questions.a: Because in India the two are often the same building. A fort's job was to protect a kingdom from invaders, but it also accommodated the residences of the ruling and military classes, and depending on its size it could hold an entire city. Since some forts therefore sheltered a royal palace inside them -- as Mehrangarh, Agra and Orchha do -- the chapter treats the two categories together rather than separating them.

questions.a: They are blue because a solution of copper sulphate mixed with lime is applied to the walls, which is said to repel termites. Apart from the colour, Jodhpur's older quarters have meandering streets, open courtyards, jali windows for ventilation, thick walls and balconies, and the chapter says all of these work together to keep the houses cool.

questions.q: Shah Jahan was imprisoned until his death by his son Aurangzeb in one of the Agra fort's marble palaces. What is striking about that, given the chapter's account of his work at the fort?
questions.a: What is striking is that he was shut up in a building he himself had made. Shah Jahan was fond of marble and replaced many of Akbar's sandstone buildings at the fort with marble ones, the palaces in particular, and it was in one of those very palaces -- the Musamman Burj, from which the Taj Mahal can be seen in the distance -- that his son Aurangzeb confined him until he died. The luxury he had built became his prison.
s: He had himself replaced the sandstone palaces with marble ones out of his liking for marble

questions.q: A ruler must choose where to put a new fort. Using this section, give three things he would consider and the reason for each.
questions.a: First, position relative to routes: forts were strategically located near important land or sea routes, because a fort guards what passes it and cannot guard what never comes near. Second, height: a site atop a hill commands a view of the plains below, so an approaching force is seen long before it arrives -- Mehrangarh stands above Jodhpur for exactly that reason. Third, material: Mehrangarh used massive blocks of locally sourced red sandstone, and even Akbar's Agra fort drew its stone from Dholpur only about 60 km away, because moving enough stone for a fort any further is impractical.
s: Nearness to important land or sea routes, since a fort guards what passes it
A hilltop site commanding a view of the plains below, to see an enemy coming
Availability of building stone nearby, as at Mehrangarh and Agra

questions.q: A district has an old hill fort with a ruined palace inside it. Using what the chapter says about Mehrangarh and the Agra fort, propose how it might be brought back into use, and say what each proposal would preserve.
questions.a: Sample: First, turn part of it into a museum, as has been done with many parts of Mehrangarh, which the chapter says preserves and showcases the fort's and the region's cultural heritage -- that keeps the rooms in repair by giving them a daily use and pays for the repair out of visitors. Second, keep the quarters legible rather than emptying them: label the areas for the royal family, the separate quarters for men and women, the staff quarters, the stables and the barracks, because the plan is the evidence of how a court actually lived, and an unlabelled ruin loses that. Third, repair what has been damaged but do not disguise the damage, since the Agra fort's story includes Shah Jahan's marble replacing Akbar's sandstone and later demolition by East India Company troops in the 19th century; a fort that hides its later history teaches only half of it.
s: A museum use, as at Mehrangarh, to preserve and showcase the heritage and fund upkeep
Keeping the internal plan legible -- royal areas, separate quarters, staff quarters, stables, barracks
Repairing without erasing later history, citing the Agra fort's rebuildings and demolitions

questions.q: Follow the Agra fort through its changes -- a brick fort fallen to ruin, Akbar's rebuilding, Shah Jahan's marble, Aurangzeb's prisoner, the East India Company's troops. What does the building itself record?
questions.a: Sample: It records a sequence of powers, each leaving its own layer. The brick ruin shows there was something worth holding at Agra before the Mughals ever came. Akbar's rebuilding in red sandstone from Dholpur, with palaces, gardens, living quarters and halls for public and private audiences, records the decision to make Agra an imperial capital. Shah Jahan's marble replacing that sandstone records a change of taste and of wealth within the same dynasty. His imprisonment there by Aurangzeb records the dynasty turning on itself. The destruction of many buildings by East India Company troops in the 19th century records the arrival of a power that had no use for the place as a court. So the fort is not one building from one moment; it is a stack of decisions, and the gaps in it are as much evidence as the walls.
s: The earlier brick fort and Akbar's rebuilding in Dholpur sandstone as an imperial capital
Shah Jahan's marble and then his imprisonment there by Aurangzeb
Nineteenth-century destruction by East India Company troops, and the conclusion that the fort is a layered record

questions.q: Compare the Mehrangarh Fort with the Mysuru Palace -- period, purpose, material and style. What had changed in what a ruler wanted from a great building?
questions.a: Sample: Mehrangarh was begun in the mid-15th century and expanded by Rajput rulers for two centuries; it is a fortress first, of massive blocks of locally sourced red sandstone, standing above Jodhpur to command the plain, with barracks and stables beside the royal quarters. The Mysuru Palace was built early in the 20th century after fire destroyed the previous wooden palace; it is a residence, not a defence, in the Indo-Saracenic style, and its glories are carved wooden doors, ornate ceiling paintings, stained-glass windows, a golden throne shown at Dasara and nearly 100,000 lights on Sunday evenings. What has changed is what the building is for: by 1900 a ruler no longer needed to survive a siege, so the money that once went into walls went into display, ceremony and the public spectacle of festivals. The earlier building answers an enemy; the later one answers an audience.
s: Mehrangarh: mid-15th century onward, defensive, local red sandstone, hilltop above Jodhpur
Mysuru: early 20th century, residential and ceremonial, Indo-Saracenic, wooden doors, stained glass, golden throne, lights
The conclusion: defence gives way to display and public ceremony as the purpose of a great building

questions.q: Many parts of the Mehrangarh Fort have been converted into a museum. Is that the best way to preserve such a building? Argue both ways and give your verdict.
questions.a: Sample: In favour: the chapter says the conversion preserves and showcases the fort's and Rajasthan's cultural heritage, a building in daily use is maintained rather than left to rot, and visitors who can walk through the royal areas, the separate quarters and the stables understand a court far better than any book will teach them. Against: a museum freezes a fort into an exhibit, the fittings and routines of a living household disappear behind glass and rope, and heavy visitor traffic itself wears a five-hundred-year-old structure. My verdict is that it is the best available option for a building this large, because nothing else generates the money and the reason to keep it standing -- but only if the fort is kept legible as a fort, with its barracks, stables and quarters explained where they stand, rather than being emptied out into display cases.
s: The case for: upkeep, funding and public understanding, as the chapter says of Mehrangarh
The case against: freezing a living building into an exhibit, and visitor wear
A verdict with a condition, such as keeping the fort readable as a fort

Label three, 'The stone decides': samples of Mehrangarh's locally sourced red sandstone, Dholpur sandstone from Agra and Shah Jahan's marble, captioned to show that a fort's colour and finish record both what lay nearby and what its ruler could afford to bring.
s: A label on who lived in a fort, using Mehrangarh's internal quarters
A label on cooling, using the Agra fountains and Jodhpur's house features
